one_line: The homepage is a single fall of sand — scrolling empties an hourglass, and only when it runs out does the liquid-glass nav materialise and the brand say its own name — so the site's central mechanic and its hardest performance problem are solved by the same decision.
big_idea:
The organising idea is a rule, not a motif: **scroll is the only clock on this site, with exactly one exception.**

Everything on the page that behaves temporally — the sand level in the hourglass, the raking specular highlight travelling the rim of the nav pill, the copy that replaces itself as the hero drains, the light angle in the hero — is driven by scroll position. The user is in control of time. There is precisely **one** element driven by real wall-clock time: the drop countdown. That is time the user does not control. The whole brand tension lives in that single contrast, and the site is built so you can feel it.

That maps directly onto the corrected brand meaning. "EARN EVERY SECOND" and "TIME WON'T WAIT" are the grind — that is the scrollable part, the part you put the work into. "OUR TIME" is the arrival — it is what the page says when the glass has emptied. The homepage is therefore a narrative arc with a beginning and an end, not a stack of sections: you scroll through the overtime and you land in our time. Because "OUR" is collective, the copy at the end shifts from imperative ("EARN EVERY SECOND.") to declarative and shared ("OUR TIME.") — there is no second-person hustle copy anywhere on the site.

Why this fits OUR TIME and not a generic time-themed brand:

1. **The mechanic is already printed on the product.** The hero garment is the navy tee with the distressed-engraving hourglass back-print. The scroll-scrubbed hourglass is not a decorative device bolted onto a clothing site — it is the graphic the customer is about to buy, animated once, and then the sequence match-cuts straight into a still of that exact print on the exact garment. The site's biggest technical moment resolves into the product. That is the difference between a concept and a gimmick.

2. **It solves the brief's hardest engineering collision by making it a design beat.** The research is unambiguous: `backdrop-filter` over animating content re-rasterises every frame, and `position: fixed` + backdrop-filter is the worst case on iOS. So the nav is **solid smoked black while it is over the moving hourglass, and cross-fades to glass the moment the sequence ends**. That is mitigation 2 from the performance brief (opacity cross-fade of two pre-blurred layers) and it is also the concept's punctuation: the glass empties, and the glass arrives. The perf fix and the art direction are the same line of code.

3. **It gives the restraint rules teeth.** "One real-time element" is a law that automatically kills the ticking-clock cursor, the live-time header readout, the sand-particle canvas, the hourglass spinner and the clock-hand scroll indicator — every single item on the teardown's cliché ranking. I am not asking a designer to show taste later; the rule does it.

4. **Two timers, two registers.** The hype timer counts down to the drop **closing**, Corteiz-style inverted scarcity, not to it opening. The second timer is the dispatch cutoff in the cart and on the PDP ("ORDER IN 04:12 FOR NEXT-DAY DISPATCH") — Represent's unhyped, functional use. A brand that only uses countdowns to manufacture urgency reads as a Shopify app. A brand that also uses one to tell you something useful reads as a brand that means it.

The concept is called THE GLASS EMPTIES because both glasses are in it.
time_theme:
Structurally, not decoratively. Five load-bearing expressions, in descending order of how much of the build they touch:

**1. The homepage is one fall of sand, and the copy is its three beats.**
The hero is a 260vh pinned section containing a scroll-scrubbed 123-frame hourglass render. The copy line in the bottom-left changes at two scroll thresholds, cross-faded on opacity (never per-letter, never typewriter):
- 0–33% of the pin: `EARN EVERY SECOND.`
- 33–72%: `TIME WON'T WAIT.`
- 72–100%, as the top bulb empties: `OUR TIME.`
That is the brand's whole semantic arc — grind → pressure → arrival — delivered by scroll distance. No section headings needed to explain it.

**2. The nav's state is a function of elapsed time.** Solid over the hero (time still running), glass afterwards (time's up). And the raking specular angle `--ot-light` is bound to sand level during the pin and to page progress after it, so the highlight crosses the pill like a second hand crossing a watch face. One registered custom property, works in every browser including Safari and Firefox, costs nothing, and is the single most bespoke-feeling detail in the build.

**3. Sections carry lap splits, not numbers.** In the left gutter (desktop) / above the section rule (mobile), each section is labelled with a fixed split time in 10px mono: `00:00`, `02:00`, `02:41`, `04:15`, `06:00`, `24:00`. These are **editorial constants baked into the content, not a live percentage** — they change on section entry, they never interpolate. It reads as a race split or a film timecode, not a progress bar. The footer is `24:00` because the brand owns "24 / 7".

**4. The countdown is structural, not ornamental.** It is a full section with its own ground colour, it inverts scarcity (counts to the drop *closing*), it is content-managed rather than hardcoded, it is hidden by a `:has()` guard until it has resolved so you never see a flash of `00:00:00`, and on expiry it swaps in-place into a live `ENTER THE DROP →` link rather than sitting at zero. `data-timezone="store"` so it is one global moment.

**5. The catalogue's own vocabulary is temporal.** Drops are numbered (`DROP 001`), not seasons. Product cards for sold-out pieces read `TIME'S UP` rather than `SOLD OUT` — the one place the brand voice is allowed to replace a functional word, because the meaning is unambiguous and it is a designed state, not an error state. Restock reads `BACK ON THE CLOCK`. Nothing else in the UI is renamed; renaming "Add to bag" would be cute and would cost conversions.

**Where I refuse to take it:** there is no clock face anywhere in the interface. The Roman-numeral clock print and the engraved wristwatch stay on the garments and appear on the site only as photographed product. An SVG clock face in a hero is the single most-generated shape in the "time-themed website" prompt space and it would undo everything above.

art_direction.palette:
Every value is either sampled from the supplied renders or explicitly derived from one. Nothing is invented.

**Grounds**
- `--ot-ground: #0F0F0F` — the page background everywhere. Textured near-black, NOT #000, NOT slate-900, NOT zinc-950.
- `--ot-void: #000000` — photographic backdrop only. Lives inside image frames and the hero canvas letterbox. Never a CSS background for a section.
- `--ot-deep: #10141E` — the drop section's ground. Derived, `color-mix(in oklab, #141B2C 62%, #0F0F0F)`. A navy-leaning near-black so the navy product reads against it instead of vanishing.
- `--ot-sand: #CFC2B4` — the light ground. Used for exactly one section (WORLD / the engraving) and for the washed-black product's photographic set.

**Ink**
- `--ot-bone: #FAF6F6` — the primary ink on dark. Warm, not #FFF. 17.9:1 on ground. This is the logo white; using true white anywhere would make the logo look dirty.
- `--ot-grey: #A7A5A4` — secondary ink. 7.8:1 on ground. Captions, sizes, prices-when-struck.
- `--ot-ground` on `--ot-sand` = 11:1 — the inverted section is fully legible.

**Product colours (never used as UI colours — these exist so swatch chips are true)**
`#141B2C` navy tee · `#141925` navy short · `#171717` washed black · `#A7A5A4` washed grey · `#54647E` washed denim · `#DFDDDE` off-white · `#CFC2B4` cream/sand. Later drops add forest green and brown/taupe as swatch tokens only.

**THE CRITICAL FINDING, checked not assumed:** `#171717` washed black on `#0F0F0F` ground is **1.07:1**. It is invisible. So there is a hard art-direction law: **the washed-black garment is never photographed or placed on the near-black ground.** It is always on sand `#CFC2B4` or bone. Its swatch chip gets a 1px `--ot-grey` hairline ring so it does not disappear in the filter bar either. This is the kind of thing that ruins a launch and it is caught here.

**The one accent, and the decision behind it**
The most saturated colour the brand owns is `#54647E`, a muted slate-denim. Introducing any new hue would instantly make the *website* the loudest thing in the brand — so no new hue is introduced. `--ot-denim: #54647E` is the site's only accent and it has exactly **one** job: the live drop countdown. Nothing else. Not buttons, not links, not hover states, not focus rings (those are bone).

Contrast maths, checked: denim on ground is **3.2:1** — below AA for body text. So denim is only ever used at ≥24px or as a non-text element, which is fine because it appears only as the countdown's colon separators and the `LIVE` state chip. Bone on a denim *fill* is **5.59:1**, so the `LIVE` chip is a filled denim pill with bone text, which passes. Coloured denim text at body size is banned in the token comments.

**No gradients. Anywhere.** Not on buttons, not on headings, not as a scrim, not as a hero mesh. Section-to-section transitions are hard cuts between grounds. The only soft luminance ramps on the site are inside photographs and the hero render, where they came from a camera or a light.

**Radius poles.** `0` on everything — cards, inputs, chips, the cart drawer, images. The only exceptions are `999px` on the nav pill and on the colour swatch chips. Square or pill; nothing in between. No `rounded-2xl`.
art_direction.typography:
Two optical sizes of one grotesque, one mono, and one engraved serif used exactly once. The wordmark is never a webfont.

**Display — Neue Haas Grotesk Display Pro, 55 Roman and 65 Medium.**
Monotype/Linotype, licensed as a webfont through Monotype Fonts or MyFonts on a pageview tier (a new label sits in the lowest band; budget £150–£400 one-off for two weights). This is the real Helvetica by Christian Schwartz, and the *Display* optical cut is genuinely different from the text cut — tighter spacing, finer joins, drawn for 40px+. Using both optical sizes of one family is the two-register discipline (Fear of God: Condensed + Optima; Cole Buxton: Akkurat Light + Bold) without importing a second personality. It is also deliberately *not* Söhne (Aimé Leon Dore's), *not* Akkurat (Cole Buxton's), *not* Favorit (SSENSE/Adanola's) — the three faces this category has already claimed.

**Text/UI — Neue Haas Grotesk Text Pro, 55 Roman and 75 Bold.** Same licence purchase.

**Micro/data — ABC Diatype Mono, Regular only.** Dinamo, webfont licence by pageviews, roughly €90–150 for one style at launch traffic. Used at 10–11px for every label, lap split, size, filter, swatch name, countdown legend and table figure. Slashed zero via `font-feature-settings: "zero" 1, "tnum" 1` — a detail no template ships.

**The engraved serif — Redaction 35, used ONCE.** OFL, free, by Titus Kaphar and Jeremy Mickel/Forest Young. It is a serif drawn in graded states of degradation, which is literally the distressed-engraving register of the hourglass back-print. It sets the single line of brand copy in the WORLD section and appears nowhere else on the site. One face, one line, one place — scarcity is what stops it reading as decoration.

**The wordmark — SVG, always.** "OUR TIME" set in the supplied thin wide-tracked art is shipped as an inline SVG path, not as type. This is the correct engineering answer to the brief's fragility warning: a path cannot collapse its word space, cannot be re-hyphenated, cannot fall back to a system font mid-load. It appears in exactly **two** places: the pre-hero first paint, and the footer lockup. Nowhere else. Where "OUR TIME" appears in running copy it is real text with `letter-spacing: .38em; word-spacing: .95em;` declared explicitly and a Playwright regression test that screenshots it — never left to a default.

**Zero-budget plan B if the licence spend is refused:** Instrument Sans (OFL) for display and text with a custom `font-variation-settings` optical tweak, Martian Mono (OFL) for micro, Redaction unchanged. Banned outright: Inter, Poppins, Montserrat, DM Sans, Manrope, Space Grotesk, Plus Jakarta Sans — Trapstar and Kith both run Inter and both look like defaults despite being real brands.

**The type scale, and the law that governs it: tracking inverts with size.** Tight or zero at display size, wide at micro size, never both.
```css
--t-display-xl: clamp(2.75rem, 7.4vw, 5.5rem);  /* 44→88px, ls -0.015em, lh 0.92 */
--t-display-l:  clamp(2rem, 4.6vw, 3.25rem);    /* 32→52px, ls -0.01em,  lh 1.0  */
--t-head:       clamp(1.25rem, 2vw, 1.5rem);    /* ls 0,    lh 1.15 */
--t-body:       clamp(0.9375rem, 1.1vw, 1rem);  /* 15→16px, ls 0, lh 1.55 */
--t-micro:      0.625rem;                        /* 10px, UPPERCASE, ls .15em, mono */
--t-nav:        0.6875rem;                       /* 11px, UPPERCASE, ls .12em, mono */
--t-count:      clamp(2.5rem, 9vw, 5rem);        /* ls 0, tabular-nums, Display 65 */
```
The 92px ceiling is deliberate — ALD's largest is 5.75rem. Resisting 20vw display type is most of what separates art direction from a landing-page template. The wide-tracked treatment lives at 10px on labels attached to objects (sizes, colourway names, drop numbers, lap splits) and **never** on a headline, which is exactly where the thin OUR TIME wordmark would otherwise get misused.

**No eyebrow labels above section headings.** The micro-type appears on *things* — a swatch, a size, a split — not as a decorative rhythm above every H2.
art_direction.imagery:
**Three image registers, and they never mix inside one frame.**

**1. The render (one asset only).** The hourglass. Blackened-brass frame, etched glass with the distressed-engraving line quality of the back-print, warm bone sand `#FAF6F6`. Lit by a single large soft key from camera left with hard falloff to the right and no fill — the same light as every photograph on the site, so the render and the photography cut together. Sitting on `#0F0F0F` with a soft floor pool, not floating on black. Positioned right-of-centre in the 4:5 master so the desktop cover-crop reads asymmetric rather than dead-centred.

**2. The on-model photography.** Overcast, single-source, matte blacks that never crush. 35mm film grain, slight halation. The poses are a deliberate list, chosen because they are simultaneously the category's visual language, the brand's register, and the failure modes AI handles best: **backs turned, mid-stride, cropped at the jaw, hands in pockets, hood up and away, looking down.** Nobody smiles at camera. Nobody is symmetrical and front-lit. Skin is described as matte with visible pores, never "smooth". A small consistent cast — **one model for DROP 001**, built as a locked five-view character sheet and reused on every frame, with a second cast member only if the client wants a pair shot. Faces approved by the client before any volume generation.

**3. The flat-lay and the engraving.** Flat-lays stay in the product gallery, never in a hero — the whole category shows garments worn. The distressed hourglass engraving appears once, as a 1600px-wide plate bleeding off the right edge of the WORLD section at ~14% opacity, tonally flattened into the sand ground. It is texture, not an icon.

**Aspect ratios — deliberately not round numbers where it counts.** Product cards `4/5`. Hero sequence master `4/5`, cover-fit. Lookbook editorial band `1.414` (√2 — derived from paper stock, which is where engravings live). One hard-cropped `21/9` band in the lookbook that cuts the model at mid-thigh and off the frame edge. Mixing a card ratio, a paper ratio and a cinema crop is what stops the grid reading as a token set.

**Formats.** AVIF for every static photograph (best bytes, decode speed irrelevant for a single image). **WebP for the hero sequence** — AVIF decode is 5–10× slower than JPEG and the sequence does 120 sequential decodes on a mid-range Android; this is the one place AVIF is the wrong answer. Video: H.264 High `yuv420p` MP4 at ~4–6 Mbps, plus a VP9 WebM alternate. Never `.mov` (Sporty & Rich's mistake). Every video carries a designed AVIF poster, because a meaningful share of iOS Low Power Mode users will only ever see the poster.

**The disclosure line, in the footer, in 10px mono:** `CAMPAIGN IMAGERY CREATED WITH AI. ALL GARMENTS ARE REAL PRODUCTS.` Costs nothing, pre-empts the whole ASA question, and several brands now read it as a trust signal.
art_direction.motion:
**The motion language is: one thing moves at a time, and it moves because you moved.**

There is no animation library on the critical path. Native CSS `animation-timeline: view()` behind `@supports` for reveals and the one parallax layer, with a ~15-line `IntersectionObserver` fallback for Firefox. These run on the compositor and cost essentially zero INP. GSAP ScrollTrigger is dynamic-imported for exactly **one** thing — pinning the hero — because pinning with scrollbar compensation, resize and iOS rubber-band is genuinely hard and is the one place 27 KB earns its keep. No Lenis: it hijacks native scroll, adds latency by design, breaks `animation-timeline`, and overrides the user's OS scroll settings.

**THE SEVEN RESTRAINT RULES. These are build gates, not aspirations.**

1. **One scrubbed sequence per page, and only on the homepage.** The hourglass scrubs. Nothing else on the site scrubs, ever. A second sequence is self-indulgent and you will feel it on a Moto G.
2. **Exactly one element is driven by wall-clock time: the drop countdown.** Anything else that ticks, counts, sweeps or updates without user input is deleted. This rule alone removes the clock cursor, the live-time header, the count-up stats band, the sand-particle canvas and the hourglass spinner.
3. **Reveals are per-section, not per-element.** A section's content arrives as one unit, 520ms, custom cubic-bezier, ~14px of travel. No 100ms staggers, no `fade-in-up` on every child. If two adjacent sections use the same reveal, one of them changes.
4. **Nothing loops faster than 6 seconds.** Ambient video is near-still — fabric moving in wind, dust crossing a light shaft, a drawstring settling. It should read as a photograph that happens to breathe.
5. **The blur radius is never animated.** State changes on the glass are opacity cross-fades between two pre-rendered layers. A transitioning blur cannot be cached and drops to ~30fps on mobile.
6. **One glass surface per viewport.** The nav pill, or the collection filter bar, or the cart drawer scrim — never two at once. When the cart drawer opens, the pill goes solid.
7. **Lap splits do not interpolate.** They change on section entry and hold. The moment they become a continuous percentage they are a scroll-progress bar with a costume on.

**Explicitly banned, by name:** custom cursor of any kind; scroll-progress bar; count-up numbers; typewriter text; 3D tilt-on-hover cards; marquee with no information in it; parallax on more than one layer per viewport; `will-change` on anything except the single persistent nav.

**`prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` is honoured properly, not with a global kill-switch alone.** The sequence renders **one chosen frame at ~62% progress** (sand mid-fall, the best-composed frame — not frame 1), the pin is released so the section becomes normal flow, all three copy lines stack as static type, the specular angle freezes at 210°, video loses `autoplay` and gains visible controls, and the WebGL parallax never initialises. WCAG 2.3.3 names scroll parallax explicitly, and SC 2.2.2 (Level A, not AAA) governs the autoplaying lookbook loop — that one is baseline legal exposure for a UK storefront, not a nicety.

**Save-Data / `effectiveType` in {slow-2g, 2g, 3g}:** static hero frame only. No sequence, no WebGL, no ambient video. `Save-Data: on` is a request, not a hint.

page_by_page.name: 00:00 — FIRST PAINT (not a loading screen)
page_by_page.purpose: Give the one legitimate appearance of the thin OUR TIME wordmark at scale, and hand the browser a controlled LCP.
page_by_page.layout: Desktop and mobile identical: `#0F0F0F` full-bleed, the OUR TIME wordmark as inline SVG, bone, centred, capped at 420px wide desktop / 62vw mobile, optically raised to 46% viewport height. `EST. 2026` in 10px mono at the bottom edge. This is simply what the page looks like before the hero's first frame decodes — there is no artificial delay, no progress indicator, no timer. If the hero image is warm in cache it is gone in ~120ms.
page_by_page.media: None. Inline SVG only. The real `` of hero frame 1 sits behind it with `fetchpriority="high"` and a ``, and is the LCP element — a `` is not an LCP candidate, so if you skip this your LCP resolves to random nav text.
page_by_page.interaction: The wordmark cross-fades out on the hero image's `decode()` promise, 280ms. It never reappears on subsequent navigations (`sessionStorage` flag). Under `prefers-reduced-motion` it is replaced instantly with no fade.

page_by_page.name: 00:00 → 02:00 — THE HOURGLASS (the pinned scrub)
page_by_page.purpose: The site's one big moment. Deliver the brand's three-beat narrative arc as scroll distance, and set up the match cut into product.
page_by_page.layout: **Desktop:** a 260vh section with a `position: sticky; top: 0; height: 100svh` inner. The 4:5 master render is cover-fit, so on a wide viewport you get a centre band of it with the hourglass sitting right-of-centre (~62% across) — deliberately not centred. Copy block bottom-left, 64px from the edges: a 10px mono label `EST. 2026 — DROP 001` above a single `--t-display-xl` line. Lap split `00:00` in the left gutter, vertical, 10px mono, `writing-mode: vertical-rl`. Nav pill is SOLID throughout. **Mobile:** 220vh section, `100svh` sticky inner (svh, not vh, so the URL bar does not resize the pin), the same 4:5 master now cropping *tighter* so the hourglass fills more of the frame. Copy stacks at the bottom above the safe area, display line drops to `clamp(2rem,9vw,2.75rem)`. No vertical gutter split on mobile — it becomes a horizontal 10px mono rule above the copy.
page_by_page.media: **Asset HG-SEQ.** A 123-frame Blender-rendered image sequence of the hourglass draining, 30fps × 4.1s of motion, three responsive WebP tiers (1440×1800 desktop ≈ 5.0 MB, 828×1035 mobile ≈ 2.0 MB, 540×675 Save-Data ≈ 1.1 MB), plus a 12-frame 320px proxy (~36 KB) that loads first so the scrub is instantly responsive. Frame 1 also ships as a standalone AVIF for the LCP ``.
page_by_page.interaction: GSAP ScrollTrigger pins the section; a `rAF`-coalesced scroll handler maps progress → frame index → `ctx.drawImage`. Never queue a draw, always draw the latest target, `nearest()` falls back to the closest decoded frame so it can never go blank. `createImageBitmap(blob, { resizeWidth: canvas.width, resizeQuality: 'high' })` caps decoded memory at display size — the single highest-leverage line in the build (it takes the 828 tier from ~108 MiB to ~40 MiB). Sliding window: 16 frames at 828, 8 at 1440, 24 at 540, with `.close()` on evict. Fetch starts on `load` + `requestIdleCallback`, never before. Copy swaps at progress 0.33 and 0.72 by opacity. `prefers-reduced-motion`: pin released, one frame at 62%, three lines stacked static.

page_by_page.name: 02:00 — THE MATCH CUT (the garment, silent)
page_by_page.purpose: Resolve the concept into the product. The thing you just watched drain is the thing printed on the tee.
page_by_page.layout: **Desktop:** full-bleed, 100svh, a single photograph of the navy tee's back — framed at the *same crop height, same key-light angle and same subject scale* as frame 123 of the sequence, so scrolling past the pin boundary reads as a cut, not a transition. One 10px mono label bottom-left: `OVERSIZED HEAVYWEIGHT TEE — WASHED NAVY — HOURGLASS BACK PRINT`. A single bone hairline `View →` link beneath it. Nothing else. No heading. **Mobile:** same shot recomposed 4:5 portrait, 88svh, label and link stacked bottom-left. The nav pill cross-fades from solid to glass exactly here.
page_by_page.media: **Asset OT-01.** On-model still, back view, navy tee, hourglass print, near-black seamless. This is the highest-fidelity asset on the site and is generated first, because everything else is graded to match it.
page_by_page.interaction: No motion at all. This is the only full-screen section on the site with zero movement, and the stillness after 260vh of scrubbing is the point. The nav's solid→glass cross-fade fires on this section's `IntersectionObserver` entry.

page_by_page.name: 02:41 — THE RUN (the shorts, six colourways)
page_by_page.purpose: The commerce beat. Six washed sweat-short colourways as a real grid with quick-add — the drop's breadth, shown as product, not as a carousel.
page_by_page.layout: **Desktop:** ground `#0F0F0F`. Section rule at the top: a 1px bone-14% hairline with the lap split `02:41` and the label `SWEAT SHORT — SIX WASHES` sitting on it in 10px mono. 3-up grid, two rows, 40px gutter, cards at `aspect-ratio: 4/5`, `max-width: 1320px` but the grid **bleeds 40px past the container on the right** so the third column is visibly cropped by the viewport edge — breaking the symmetric-container tell. **Mobile:** 2-up grid, 12px gutter, edge-to-edge with a 16px page gutter, same 4/5. Card chrome: colourway name in 10px mono `.15em` (`WASHED DENIM`), price in text Roman, and the swatch chip. No card shadows, no radius, no borders except the washed-black chip's hairline ring.
page_by_page.media: **Assets SH-01…SH-06.** Six on-model shorts stills, identical model, identical pose, identical light, one variable changed (colour) — plus six hover frames at a different crop. The washed-black pair (SH-05) is shot on a warm sand set, never on near-black, per the 1.07:1 contrast finding.
page_by_page.interaction: Hover reveals the second shot (the near-universal category behaviour: Cole Buxton, Stüssy, Gymshark). `QuickAdd` on the card opens a 6-cell size row inline — sizes that do not exist in that colourway render as struck-through and unclickable (`not made`), sizes that exist but are out render as `TIME'S UP`. That tri-state is built on fake data from day one, because it is exactly what gets skipped and blows up on launch day. Cards reveal per-row via `animation-timeline: view()` behind `@supports`, IO fallback.

page_by_page.name: 04:15 — THE LOOKBOOK (AI video + the 3D flair)
page_by_page.purpose: Show the garments worn, in a place, moving. This is where the AI-generated video and the depth parallax do their work — and the only place on the site with more than one moving element.
page_by_page.layout: **Desktop:** an asymmetric two-column editorial, `grid-template-columns: 1.15fr 0.85fr`, 120px of vertical air. Left: a tall `1.414` (√2) still of the model in tee + shorts, carrying the depth-map 2.5D parallax. Right, offset 140px lower: a 9:16 ambient video loop, `max-height: 78svh`. Below both, full-bleed across the whole viewport, a hard-cropped `21/9` band that cuts the model at mid-thigh and off the right frame edge. **Mobile:** the 9:16 loop goes full-bleed first (it was shot for this), then the √2 still, then the 21/9 band scaled to `16/9` and allowed to scroll-crop. Parallax is disabled on mobile; the still is just a still.
page_by_page.media: **Assets LB-VID-01** (Veo 3.1 Fast, 8s, 9:16 and 16:9 cuts, `image` + `lastFrame` set to the same PNG for a seamless loop), **LB-01** (√2 still + a build-time Depth Anything V2 greyscale depth map shipped as a half-res greyscale WebP, ~12 KB), **LB-02** (21/9 crop still).
page_by_page.interaction: One `<video>` element, two `<source>`s, `media="(orientation: portrait)"` on the first — the browser picks the phone cut natively, no JS, no double download. `muted playsinline loop autoplay preload="none"`, designed AVIF poster, audio track stripped with `-an` (stronger than `muted`: a file with no audio track can never gain one and so can never be auto-paused). The parallax is ~60 lines of raw WebGL, one fullscreen quad, 6-iteration UV refinement — **not** Three.js (185 KB gz and 400–700ms of main thread before first paint). Gated on `(min-width:900px) and (pointer:fine)` and off under Save-Data. `uOffset` lerped from scroll progress and `pointermove`.

page_by_page.name: 06:00 — THE DROP (the one real clock)
page_by_page.purpose: The site's only wall-clock element. Inverted scarcity, Corteiz-style: it counts to the drop CLOSING, not opening.
page_by_page.layout: **Desktop:** ground flips to `--ot-deep #10141E` — a hard cut, no gradient. Full-bleed, ~78svh. Scroll-scrubbing needs frame-exact determinism, exact loop length, and a final frame that matches a photograph — none of which a generative video model will give you, at any price.

SPEC: Build the hourglass to match the approved HG-KEY still — blackened brass frame (Principled BSDF, metallic 1.0, roughness 0.42, subtle anisotropy), etched glass (transmission 1.0, roughness 0.08, IOR 1.52, with the distressed engraving artwork driving a roughness/bump mask), sand as a particle-free displaced mesh for the pile plus a tapered emissive-free column mesh for the falling stream. Ground plane #0F0F0F with a soft pool. One large area light camera-left at 3.2m, no fill, no rim. Camera locked, 85mm equivalent, hourglass composed at 62% across the frame in a 4:5 master so the desktop cover-crop reads asymmetric.

ANIMATION: 123 frames at 30fps (4.1s). Frames 1–100: sand falls at an eased-out rate (fast at first, decelerating — real hourglasses do not drain linearly, and the deceleration is what makes the scrub feel physical). Frames 100–118: the upper bulb empties, the column thins and breaks. Frames 119–123: the last motes land; camera holds.

tech_stack:
**Astro 5 + TypeScript + vanilla CSS. No Tailwind. No React on the critical path.**

*Why Astro:* it ships zero JavaScript by default and hydrates only the islands that need it (the canvas sequence, the cart drawer, the filter bar, the countdown). It statically generates PDPs and collection pages, which is what the SEO actually requires — a client-only SPA storefront is an own-goal. And it has a Cloudflare adapter waiting the day content moves into Shopify metaobjects, which need a server-side private token. Next.js would work; Hydrogen/Oxygen is rejected outright as the maximum-lock-in option whose framework has been rewritten under its users twice, and which gives nothing that a headless build does not.

*Why no Tailwind:* roughly half the vibe-coded tell list is literally Tailwind's defaults — `#615fff`, `slate-900`, `rounded-2xl p-6`, `shadow-lg`, the `text-sm/base/lg/xl` scale. Avoiding them while using the framework is possible and is constant vigilance. Hand-authored CSS with `@layer reset, tokens, base, components, utilities` and every value coming from a named brand token is less work than policing it, and it is why this site will not have a single `from-slate-900 via-purple-900` in it.

**Motion.** Native CSS `animation-timeline: view()` / `scroll()` behind `@supports`, with a ~15-line `IntersectionObserver` fallback for Firefox (still flagged in Release; Interop 2026 names it a focus area, so this improves on its own). These run on the compositor and cost ~0ms INP. **GSAP ScrollTrigger, dynamic-imported, for exactly one thing — pinning the hero.** Pinning with scrollbar compensation, resize handling and iOS rubber-band is genuinely hard and this is the one place 27 KB gz earns its keep. **Verify `node_modules/gsap/LICENSE.md` before commercial ship** — GSAP is free since April 2025 under Webflow, but "free" is not the same as MIT and the SPDX identifier is unverified in the research. No Lenis: it hijacks native scroll, breaks `animation-timeline`, overrides the user's OS scroll settings and is a known accessibility irritant.

**3D.** Blender as an offline renderer only. ~60 lines of raw WebGL (one fullscreen quad, two textures, 6-iteration UV refinement, ~4 KB) for the depth parallax. **No Three.js** — 185 KB gz and 400–700ms of main thread before first paint on a mid-range Android, for an effect that is a fragment shader.

**Glass.** ~60 lines of CSS, one inline `<svg>` filter, ~40 lines of JS. **Hand-rolled, no library.** Every glass library's headline feature is backdrop refraction, which does not run on the primary platform; the ones that do work cross-browser do it by cloning content, which collides fatally with video backdrops (Safari will not run SVG filters over live video). And the whole differentiation — the adaptive `data-over` tinting and the scroll-bound `--ot-light` specular — is exactly what no library gives you. The displacement-map generator lives in one module with no DOM assumptions beyond `document.createElement('canvas')`, so it ports into a Shopify theme section or a Hydrogen component untouched if the platform decision ever forces that.

**Hosting.** Cloudflare Pages. Free at this traffic, HTTP/3 by default (which the 123-frame sequence needs — on HTTP/1.1 the 6-connection limit makes it a disaster), immutable cache headers on `/seq/*`, and a Workers runtime already sitting there for the day a private Storefront token has to stay server-side. Video is pre-encoded MP4 + WebM on the same CDN rather than Shopify Files.

---

**THE COMMERCE SEAM — this is the load-bearing architectural decision, and it is what lets design start today.**

The platform is not confirmed, so nothing platform-shaped enters a component. Two interfaces:

```
components → useCommerce() → StorefrontAdapter → local-json | shopify | stripe
           → useContent()  → ContentAdapter    → local-json | metaobjects | sanity
```

Seven rules that make the seam real rather than aspirational:
1. No Shopify type and no `gid://shopify/...` string ever appears in a component. IDs are opaque branded strings (`ProductId`, `VariantId`, `CartLineId`).
2. Money is never a JS `number` in the UI — `{ amountMinor: 4500, currencyCode: 'GBP' }`, one `formatMoney()`.
3. URLs key on `handle`, never on id.
4. The front-end never computes tax, shipping or totals. It renders what the cart returns. `cost.tax: null` means "not known yet" and the UI says `CALCULATED AT CHECKOUT`.
5. Exactly one file knows the API version string (`SHOPIFY_API_VERSION = '2026-07'`). Bumping it quarterly is a one-hour job the cousin cannot do; keeping it to one constant is the mitigation.
6. Adapters return typed `CartResult` for user-visible failures and throw only for programmer errors.
7. Both adapters pass the **same conformance suite** in CI. When the Shopify adapter goes green, the swap is done. That suite is about a day of work and it is the entire insurance policy.

The domain model carries the Shopify concepts that leak into design, modelled now on fake data so they cannot force a redesign later: **variants are the sellable unit and the size×colour matrix is sparse** (so "not made" is a distinct UI state from "sold out"); **option ordering is editorial**, never alphabetised; **inventory is tri-state** — `availableForSale:false` vs `quantityAvailable:3` vs `quantityAvailable:null`, and treating null as 0 is the classic bug; `compareAtPrice` drives every strike-through; the media gallery is a union of image/video/model3d in merchant order, **video-native from the first commit** because this brand's galleries contain loops; collections are real collections with handles and SEO, not tag filters; cart lines carry their own attributes; discount codes can fail and the UI has that state.

**Launch mode before the platform is confirmed:** the local-JSON adapter's `beginCheckout` returns either an honest `{ kind: 'unavailable', reason: 'not-launched' }` with the join field, or — if he wants to take money immediately — a Shopify **cart permalink** (`https://<shop>.myshopify.com/cart/<variantId>:1,<variantId>:2`). That is a fully bespoke PDP and cart drawer handing off to a real Shopify checkout with zero SDK, zero token and zero API version. Genuinely underrated launch mode.

**Get the catalogue into a Shopify admin early regardless**, on the £1/month intro. Not because Shopify is decided, but because the admin is the thing the non-technical cousin actually operates daily — products, prices, photos, stock, discounts, orders, refunds are all path-independent — and because `catalogue.json` should be generated from real data rather than invented. The one real loss from going headless is page composition, so the announcement bar, nav links, homepage section order, the drop end-date, the hero video and the lookbook go behind `ContentAdapter` (JSON now, metaobjects later) with a one-page "what you can change yourself, and what needs me" note. Don't pretend that loss isn't real; budget a day for it.

**Performance budget, enforced in CI via Lighthouse-CI on a throttled mid-range profile:** LCP ≤ 2.0s (stricter than the 2.5s threshold, for headroom), INP ≤ 200ms, CLS ≤ 0.05, total JS ≤ 45 KB gz on the homepage excluding the dynamic-imported GSAP, total page weight at first interaction ≤ 1.4 MB with the sequence excluded because it is deferred past `load`. A build that breaks a budget fails the PR.

I ran this proposal against the teardown's 61-item tell list. Here is what specifically survives it, and the places where I had to change a decision because of it.

**Colour.** Zero gradients anywhere on the site — not on a button, not on a heading, not as a scrim, not as a hero mesh. Section transitions are hard cuts between grounds. The page ground is `#0F0F0F` sampled from the client's own renders, not `slate-900` `#0f172b` and not `zinc-950`. There is one accent, `#54647E`, it is a colour the brand already owns on a garment, and it is used for exactly one element. No coloured glow under anything. Tokens are named for materials (`--ot-bone`, `--ot-sand`, `--ot-denim`, `--ot-ground`), never `--primary/--secondary/--accent`.

**Typography.** No Inter, no Poppins, no Montserrat, no DM Sans, no Space Grotesk — Trapstar and Kith both run Inter and both look like defaults despite being real brands, which proves the tell is about *defaults*, not about AI. Licensed Neue Haas Grotesk in two optical sizes, one mono, one degraded serif used once. No font size comes from the Tailwind scale; every one is a `clamp()` with a stated pixel range. **The tracking inverts with size** — `.15em` at 10px on labels attached to objects, `-0.015em` at 88px on display — which is precisely where the thin wide OUR TIME wordmark would otherwise be misused as a headline face. Display caps at 92px; I am not doing 20vw. No eyebrow label above every section heading. No emoji anywhere, in any surface, including the favicon.

**Layout.** No centred hero with a one-line headline and two buttons. No Features/Testimonials/FAQ/CTA rhythm. No three-up card grid with length-equalised copy. No stats band, no logo strip, no numbered `01/02/03` step timeline, no badge pill above the H1, no information-free marquee. Radius is `0` everywhere except two pill exceptions — square or pill, committed, never a polite 8px. The footer has **three** columns and the newsletter is not in the fourth, because it lives in the drop section where it means something. The colourway grid **bleeds 40px past its container** so the right-hand column is cropped by the viewport — the symmetric max-width container on every section is tell #30 and breaking it once, deliberately, is what an art director does.

**Motion.** No custom cursor of any kind — and specifically not the ticking-clock cursor, which is the single most obvious idea available to this brief and which fails four tells simultaneously (custom cursor, literal metaphor, meaningless motion, dead on touch). No scroll-progress bar. No count-ups, no typewriter, no 3D tilt cards. Reveals are per-section with one custom easing, not `fade-in-up` on every element at 100ms staggers. `prefers-reduced-motion` is honoured with a *designed* reduced state — one chosen frame at 62% progress, not frame 1 — rather than a global `animation-duration: 0.01ms` sledgehammer alone.

**Imagery and copy.** The AI models are prompted explicitly against the tells: matte skin with visible pores rather than "not plastic", backs turned and faces cropped at the jaw, nobody smiling at camera, overcast single-source light, unbranded footwear. Flat-lays never appear in a hero — this category shows garments worn. Copy never says "Elevate your everyday" or "Where style meets comfort"; the only copy on the homepage is the brand's own four lines plus product names. No invented testimonials. And there are real numbers on the page: measured colour names, a real drop date, a real dispatch cutoff, `EST. 2026`.

**Where the checklist actually changed my design, not just confirmed it:**

1. I wanted a full-bleed glass bar. The teardown found **zero** streetwear brands blurring their navigation, and the performance research found `position: fixed` + `backdrop-filter` is the worst case on iOS. Both point the same way, so it became a 560px pill — which is also Palace's verified precedent and the more premium look.
2. I wanted the specular sweep to be the scroll indicator. That is a scroll-progress bar in fancy dress (tell #39). It became a highlight on an object instead, and the lap splits — which do the same job — were demoted to static per-section constants that never interpolate.
3. I wanted to morph the hourglass into the tee's back print. A cut is more premium than a transition, and morphs are where CGI starts to look like CGI. It became a **match cut** — same crop, same light angle, same subject scale across a hard boundary — which is harder to execute and much better.
4. I wanted the tessellated OT pattern as a page background. It is a great garment pattern and visual noise behind text. It does not appear on the site at all except as photographed product.
5. I checked the contrast rather than assuming it, and found `#171717` washed black on `#0F0F0F` is **1.07:1**. That produced a hard art-direction law — the washed-black garment is never shot or placed on the near-black ground — which is now baked into the SH-05 generation prompt. That is the kind of thing that ruins a launch and no template would ever catch it.

**The single test every decision is held against:** *would this exist if the brand had a full-time art director and no AI tools?* Corteiz's 12px yellow Courier passes that test. A ticking-clock cursor does not.
risks: **The whole concept rests on one Blender render being beautiful, and I cannot promise that from here.** If the hourglass sequence looks like a stock 3D asset, 260vh of pinned scroll becomes the most expensive gimmick on the internet and the site is worse than a simple one would have been. The mitigation is structural: the client approves a single still (HG-KEY) before 123 frames are rendered, and the fallback if it fails is to cut the pin to 140vh and treat the sequence as a short reveal rather than the spine. But the honest version is that this direction has a single point of failure and this is it.

**Pinning on iOS is a known time sink.** GSAP ScrollTrigger + URL-bar show/hide + rubber-band scrolling is genuinely fiddly. `100svh` and a debounced resize handle most of it, but budget a full day of on-device debugging and expect the pin boundary to need hand-tuning per breakpoint. This will pass on a laptop and misbehave on the client's phone — exactly the failure mode the whole brief is trying to avoid.

**The lap splits sit one design decision away from being a scroll-progress bar.** They earn their place only while they are static editorial constants. The moment someone 'improves' them into a live percentage, they become tell #39 and take the site's credibility with them. This needs to be written into the component as a comment, not just remembered.

**Tier 1 refraction may never ship on iPhone, and iPhone is where the traffic is.** WebKit bug 245510 is status NEW, PR 68614 is open and `merging-blocked` with changes requested, and the standards work (svgwg#1142) has no vendor responses. So roughly 85% of this audience will never see the effect the client specifically asked for by name. The architecture handles it — Tier 2 carries the whole identity and nothing looks missing — but the *conversation* with the client needs to happen before build, not after. Re-check bug 245510 before shipping.

**`prefers-reduced-transparency` does not work in Safari, so a user who has explicitly asked their iPhone to reduce transparency will still get glass.** The `--ot-scrim: .74` floor keeps it legible, and `prefers-contrast: more` is wired, but there is no honest way to fully honour that preference on Apple platforms today. Apple itself is reducing default transparency in iOS 27, which is a signal worth taking seriously.

**AI model consistency will drift across the colourway run.** The five-view character sheet plus one-variable-per-prompt discipline gets you most of the way, but six shorts colourways generated independently will not match perfectly, and mismatched skin tone or build across a six-up grid is instantly visible. The plan is to generate SH-01, approve it, and edit that output for SH-02 through SH-06 — and to accept that a virtual-try-on pass (FASHN or Vertex VTO, ~$2.50) may be needed for the full ~30-colourway matrix later. Do not promise the client a perfectly consistent grid on the first pass.

**The supplied renders contain a live brand-consistency bug and it can leak onto the site.** A number of garments are physically printed 'OVERTIME' rather than 'OUR TIME'. One stray legacy render in a product gallery undoes the entire premise. This needs a hard asset QA gate — every image checked against the corrected wordmark before it enters the repo, with a filename convention that makes legacy assets obvious — not a promise to be careful.

**Veo 3.1 is a preview product with sharp edges.** Audio is always on and always billed and cannot be disabled; generated URIs are deleted after 48 hours so the script must download in the same run; the UK/EU restriction means `personGeneration` can only be `allow_adult`, which forces image-conditioned generation rather than text-to-video for anything with a person in it; and Google's own docs contain an unresolved contradiction about `predictLongRunning` vs `generateContent`. None of this blocks the plan, but a preview API underneath a client's launch asset is a real dependency risk. Sora is not an alternative — it is removed from the OpenAI API on 24 September.

**GSAP is free but may not be MIT.** The research could not confirm the SPDX identifier because npm returned 403. This is a commercial storefront. Read `node_modules/gsap/LICENSE.md` before shipping; it is a thirty-second check and it is historically a 'GreenSock Standard License', not an open-source one.

**The 'one real-time element' law only works if it is enforced, and clients ask for more timers.** The moment there is a countdown on every product card, scarcity stops being scarcity and becomes a Shopify app — the exact thing the teardown identifies. This is a rule that will be tested, and the answer has to be no.

**The per-frame KB figures in the research are explicitly unverified for this content class.** The 2.2 MB mobile sequence budget is an estimate based on 'washed, desaturated, near-black compresses unusually well'. Measure the actual WebP output before committing to the budget, and be prepared to cut the frame count from 123 to ~90 rather than blow the mobile budget. On real UK cellular (3–8 Mbps on a train, not the headline 4G number) 2.2 MB is about four seconds — acceptable only because it is deferred and the static hero is already painted.

**The Chicago coordinates (41.8781 N, 87.6298 W) on the globe tee are an open question, not a fact.** If the brand is not Chicago-based this is a stray detail on a garment, and I have deliberately built no narrative on it — the site never mentions a city. But it needs answering before anyone writes an About page, because if it IS deliberate it is a much better story than anything I have proposed, and if it is not, the print should probably change.
